nameStory: Sticky Sage gets its name from the incredibly tacky, resinous coating that covers its stems and leaves. Touch this plant and you'll understand immediately why 'sticky' made it into the common name! The alternative name 'Jupiter's sage' comes from ancient Roman times, when this herb was considered worthy of the king of the gods.
description: Sticky Sage is a tall, robust perennial herb that can reach 3-4 feet in height with a bushy, upright growth habit. It belongs to the mint family and produces distinctive pale yellow flowers arranged in whorls along tall spikes. The entire plant has a somewhat wild, informal appearance with large, heart-shaped leaves that feel noticeably sticky to the touch. As an extremely rare plant in New England with only 2 recorded observations, finding one would be like discovering botanical treasure.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, heart-shaped leaves with prominent veining and a distinctly sticky, resinous surface that will leave residue on your fingers when touched

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pale yellow, two-lipped flowers typical of the mint family, arranged in whorls around tall spikes that rise above the foliage

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, bushy perennial reaching 3-4 feet with square stems characteristic of the mint family

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Every part of the plant feels noticeably sticky and resinous, with a somewhat unpleasant, medicinal smell when crushed

habitat: Given its extreme rarity in New England, Sticky Sage is most likely found in disturbed soils, garden escapes, or possibly woodland edges with rich, moist soil. In its native European range, it prefers shaded woodland areas and mountainous regions. Any New England sighting would likely be in areas with human activity or near old homesteads.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as sticky, heart-shaped leaves unfurl from the base, immediately identifiable by their tacky texture.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs mid to late summer with distinctive pale yellow flower spikes rising above the leafy growth. This is prime identification time.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seeds develop while leaves may begin to yellow but retain their characteristic stickiness until frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving no above-ground parts for identification until spring regrowth begins.

funFact: The sticky resin covering this plant is so strong that in medieval times, people actually used Sticky Sage as a natural flypaper, hanging bunches of it in kitchens and barns to catch insects!
confusionNotes: With only 2 observations in all of New England, you're more likely to confuse this with other large-leaved garden herbs like comfrey or borage. The dead giveaway is the unmistakable stickiness - no other common plant in our region has leaves this persistently tacky to the touch.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this rare Sticky Sage with our much more common native sages like Lyreleaf Sage. Most 'sages' sold in garden centers are actually different species entirely, and culinary sage (used for cooking) is yet another species - Salvia officinalis.
compareHints: Unlike our native Lyreleaf Sage which has deeply lobed leaves and purple flowers, Sticky Sage has simple heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers. It's also much taller and bushier than most other sages in our region. The sticky texture is absolutely unique among New England's sage species - if it's not sticky, it's not this species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike lyreleaf sage which has distinctive lobed basal leaves and prefers shady woods, giant blue sage has narrow, unlobed leaves and demands full sun.
Unlike other sages that might be found in New England gardens like lyreleaf sage (which has much broader, lobed leaves), mintweed has very narrow, simple leaves and a weedy appearance.
Unlike native New England sages like lyreleaf sage, chia is much taller and more robust, growing 3-5 feet compared to the 1-2 foot height of most regional relatives.
Lyreleaf sage is the only Salvia species you're likely to encounter in New England, making it unique in the region.
Unlike the native lyreleaf sage with its small purple flowers and basal rosette of leaves, anise-scented sage forms tall bushy plants with much larger, intensely blue flowers.
